newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentina urged to root out anti-Semitism in police.
newsitem.headline: Argentina urged to root out anti-Semitism in police.

text.p: The Simon Wiesenthal Centre, a Jewish organisation dedicated to hunting Nazi war criminals, urged on Thursday the governor of the province of Buenos Aires to root out anti-Semitism in the police force.
In a letter to Gov. Eduardo Duhalde, the Wiesenthal Centre said anti-Semitic acts "should be severely punished and measures should be taken to erradicate those ideas from the police ranks."
The letter, signed by the Wiesenthal Center's Argentine representative Sergio Widder, offered Duhalde help "to include education on tolerance in the police training curriculum."
The leader of Argentina's large Jewish community, Ruben Beraja, said educating the police was vital to help ward off anti-Semitic sentiment.

Last week two police officers were detained in connection with the desecration of tombs at Buenos Aires' main Jewish cemetery. Other Buenos Aires police officers were arrested last year for their alleged involvement in the 1994 bombing of a Jewish community centre that killed 86 people.
On Wednesday, the Buenos Aires security chief announced the creation of a new police unit dedicated to investigating anti-Jewish attacks.
"We will show the force is committed to the fight against discrimination. The Buenos Aires police has no animosity against the Jewish community," said Eduardo De Lazzari.
Argentina is home to about 400,000 Jews. As well as the 1994 bombing, the Israeli embassy in Buenos Aires was the target of a car bomb attack in 1992 that killed 29 people.
